\section{Introduction}\label{introduction}

Here we demonstrate the use of GLMs in modeling the frequency of auto
insurance claims. We will use the French third-party auto insurance
claims data set from the {[}CASdatasets package{]}
(\url{https://cas.uqam.ca/}). GLMs are a natural choice for modeling
claim frequency: they work well with distributions that insurance claims
are often assumed to fit, they can handle complex trends, and they are
easily interpretable and explainable.

In the future, I hope to investigate and compare different models for
frequency of claims, including machine learning methods such as random
forests and neural networks. {[}Colella and Jones{]}
(\url{https://eforum.casact.org/article/73245-machine-learning-and-ratemaking-assessing-performance-of-four-popular-algorithms-for-modeling-auto-insurance-pure-premium})
performed a similar comparison for modeling pure premium on the same
dataset. I aim to expand their analysis by using the same algorithms to
model frequency and severity separately, as is typical when using GLMs
to predict pure premium for insurance claims in practice.

We begin by making a train/test split and taking an initial look at the
data. The set we are looking at is freMTPL2freq, which has the following
columns:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{IDpol:} An ID number associated with each policy holder.
\item
  \emph{ClaimNb:} The number of claims filed under each policy. This is
  the target variable that we aim to model.
\item
  \emph{Exposure:} The amount of time a policy is active, measured in
  years. Since our aim is to model frequency, we will use this to weight
  the number of claims filed; one claim in six months should be
  considered the same frequency as two claims in one year.
\item
  \emph{VehPower:} A number representing the covered vehicle's power,
  with higher values indicating more power.
\item
  \emph{VehAge:} The vehicle's age in years.
\item
  \emph{DrivAge:} The insured driver's age in years.
\item
  \emph{BonusMalus:} In France, auto insurance policies have a
  ``bonus-malus system'' which raises or lowers premiums based on
  previous claims made on a policy. A bonus-malus of 100 is the default.
  A number less than 100 indicates that a driver has not had any claims
  for a long time, so they pay less, while a number greater than 100
  indicates the opposite. For our purposes this is a numerical indicator
  of their driving record.
\item
  \emph{VehBrand:} A categorical indicator for the vehicle's
  manufacturer.
\item
  \emph{VehGas:} Diesel or Regular per the vehicle.
\item
  \emph{Area:} A category related to population density where the
  insured driver lives.
\item
  \emph{Density:} Population density where the insured driver lives.
\item
  \emph{Region:} Policy region in France where the insured driver lives.
\end{itemize}

\section{Exploratory data analysis}\label{exploratory-data-analysis}

We aim to investigate claim frequency, so first we examine the
distribution of claim numbers for the policies in our data set. We
should also normalize by dividing by the exposure column to examine the
true claim frequency we get from each policy. A quick look for outliers
reveals something interesting right away.

The highest frequencies seem to come from policies that are active for a
very short amount of time. Time here is measured in years, so a policy
with an exposure of .0027 is active for only around one day (this is
very close to 1/365). This may strike one as unusual; such a policy
could have been cancelled by the insurer, or perhaps it could be
fraudulent. We will try to control for these outliers in our modeling.

We also examine the other variables and how they relate to claim
frequency. The outliers can make these plots hard to read, so it will be
useful to graph them against the raw number of claims as well. Jitter
plots can make the trends more visible, as many policies have the exact
same number of claims (with most having zero). Observe the following
example with plotting population density against claims:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{(Policies,}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{),}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x=}\NormalTok{Density,}\AttributeTok{y=}\NormalTok{ClaimNormalized)) }\SpecialCharTok{+} \FunctionTok{geom\_point}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{position =} \StringTok{"jitter"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{size =} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{shape=} \StringTok{"cross"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{actuarialproject_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-5-1.pdf}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{(Policies,}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{),}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x=}\NormalTok{Density,}\AttributeTok{y=}\NormalTok{ClaimNb)) }\SpecialCharTok{+} \FunctionTok{geom\_point}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{position =} \StringTok{"jitter"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{size =} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{shape=} \StringTok{"cross"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{actuarialproject_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-5-2.pdf}}

Another advantage of swarm plots is that they can give us an idea of the
distribution of both variables. We can see that there are a lot of
policies that have population density 0, which may denote an unknown
population density.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#ggplot(head(Policies,10000),aes(x=DrivAge,y=ClaimNormalized)) + geom\_point(position = "jitter", size = 1, shape= "cross")}
\CommentTok{\#ggplot(head(Policies,10000),aes(x=Density,y=ClaimNormalized)) + geom\_point(position = "jitter", size = 1, shape= "cross")}
\CommentTok{\#ggplot(head(Policies,10000) \%\textgreater{}\% filter(ClaimNormalized \textless{} 25),aes(x=Density,y=ClaimNormalized)) + geom\_point(position = "jitter", size = 1, shape= "cross")}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

We can see that there are much less vehicles in the data set with higher
power. We may benefit from some larger groupings here as well.

For many of our numerical (continuous or integer) variables, we will
want to group many values together and treat them as categorical
variables. The standard behavior of a GLM is to model these with a
single linear coefficient before the linking function is applied, so
grouping (also called binning) can help model more complicated
relationships. We demonstrate by binning driver age and visualizing
those groups with claim frequency:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Policies }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{AgeBracket =} \FunctionTok{cut}\NormalTok{(Policies}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{DrivAge, }\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{17}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{21}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{27}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{45}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{75}\NormalTok{,}\ConstantTok{Inf}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{include.lowest =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{right=}\ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{group\_by}\NormalTok{(AgeBracket) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{summarize}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{AvgClaims =} \FunctionTok{mean}\NormalTok{(ClaimNormalized)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{plot}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x=}\NormalTok{AgeBracket, }\AttributeTok{y=}\NormalTok{AvgClaims))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{actuarialproject_files/figure-latex/unnamed-chunk-11-1.pdf}}

\section{Model selection}\label{model-selection}

We must consider which linking function to use in our GLM. It is typical
to assume that claim frequency follows a Poisson distribution. To test
that assumption, we check how close the variance and average value are
to each other.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\#PoliciesGlm \textless{}{-} Policies}
\CommentTok{\#PoliciesGlm$AGEDRIVER \textless{}{-} cut(Policies$DrivAge,c(17,22,26,42,74,Inf))}
\CommentTok{\#PoliciesGlm$AGECAR \textless{}{-} cut(Policies$VehAge,c(0,1,4,15,Inf), include.lowest = TRUE)}
\CommentTok{\#PoliciesGlm$DENSITY \textless{}{-} cut(Policies$Density,c(0,40,200,500,4500,Inf),include.lowest = TRUE)}

\NormalTok{vY }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ Policies}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ClaimNb}
\NormalTok{vE }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ Policies}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{Exposure}
\NormalTok{m }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(vY)}\SpecialCharTok{/}\FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(vE)}
\NormalTok{v }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{((vY}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{m}\SpecialCharTok{*}\NormalTok{vE)}\SpecialCharTok{\^{}}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}\SpecialCharTok{/}\FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(vE)}
\FunctionTok{cat}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"average ="}\NormalTok{,m,}\StringTok{" variance ="}\NormalTok{,v,}\StringTok{"phi ="}\NormalTok{,v}\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{m,}\StringTok{"}\SpecialCharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
## average = 0.07370575  variance = 0.08112898 phi = 1.100714
\end{verbatim}

They are very close, yet variance is slightly higher than mean. Using a
poisson distribution is appropriate here.

With our linking function chosen for now, we turn our attention to the
variables our model will use as input. Many of our variables are
categorical, which makes them easy to use in GLM modeling. For those
which are numerical, it is often wise to bin them and treat them as
categorical variables, especially when they vary in a complex way with
respect to the target variable. We discuss specific choices for each
numerical variable below:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \emph{Driver age:} This variable has a specific behavior where
  frequency is highly increased for young drivers, and relatively steady
  starting at around age 26. Above, we were able to demonstrate how to
  capture that behavior with binning, and we will use those same bins in
  our model.
\item
  \emph{Vehicle age:} We will bin cars in their first year separately
  from cars 1 to 3 years old to capture the effect we see in the graph
  above. After 4 years of age, the data becomes much more sparse, so we
  will make much larger bin to reduce potential variance in our model.
\item
  \emph{Vehicle power:} Aside from a couple of outliers for higher power
  vehicles, there seems to be a fairly steady trend of higher power
  vehicles having lower frequency. We will not bin this variable.
\item
  \emph{Density:} Policies with low density seem to have a higher claim
  frequency, so we will aim to group them together. Otherwise we will
  organize our bins so that they each capture a large amount of data -
  in particular as densities get higher, there seem to be less density
  values which have claims, so bins will need to be larger.
\item
  \emph{Bonus-malus:} Because claims are so rare, most drivers will have
  a bonus-malus of under 100. We will group all drivers with bonus-malus
  of over 100 together to account for scarcity of data, and have two
  seperate groups for under 100.
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{PoliciesGLM }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}}\NormalTok{ Policies }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%} 
  \FunctionTok{filter}\NormalTok{(Exposure }\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{/}\DecValTok{13}\NormalTok{, ClaimNb }\SpecialCharTok{\textless{}} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{DrivAgeBracket =} \FunctionTok{cut}\NormalTok{(DrivAge, }\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{17}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{21}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{27}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{45}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{75}\NormalTok{,}\ConstantTok{Inf}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{include.lowest =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{right=}\ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{VehAgeBracket =} \FunctionTok{cut}\NormalTok{(VehAge,}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{,}\ConstantTok{Inf}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{include.lowest =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{DensityBracket =} \FunctionTok{cut}\NormalTok{(Density,}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{40}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{200}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{500}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{5000}\NormalTok{,}\ConstantTok{Inf}\NormalTok{),}\AttributeTok{include.lowest =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{\%\textgreater{}\%}
  \FunctionTok{mutate}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{BonusMalusBracket =} \FunctionTok{cut}\NormalTok{(BonusMalus,}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{50}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{75}\NormalTok{,}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{,}\ConstantTok{Inf}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{include.lowest =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{))}
  
  
  
  
\NormalTok{model1 }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(ClaimNb}\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{DrivAgeBracket}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{VehAgeBracket}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{DensityBracket}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{VehPower }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ VehBrand}\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{VehGas }\SpecialCharTok{+} 
\NormalTok{            Area }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ Region }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ BonusMalusBracket, }\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ quasipoisson, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ PoliciesGLM, }\AttributeTok{weights =}\NormalTok{ Exposure)}
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(model1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The model summary given to us by R can provide a wealth of information.
It gives us the value of the coefficient assigned to each variable under
the Estimate column. For instance, the Driver age bracket for ages 21
through 26 has an estimate of -.42, indicating that drivers of age 21
through 26 are much less likely to have claims than the default (the
first category, or drivers aged 18 through 20). It also gives
statistical significance values, which indicate how likely it would be
to see such an effect from that variable given the training data if that
variable had no effect on the data. Very high significance factors
indicate that the variable might not be useful for modeling; it may
produce more noise than signal.

In particular, the significance factors for the Area variable are quite
high, and based off of the definitions for each variable, we may be able
to get a more accurate account for what the Area variable is supposed to
represent by including Density in our model anyway.

Below, we will test three different versions of our model: one which
uses all of our variables, one which leaves out Area but uses the rest,
and a very simple baseline model which only uses two variables which
have an extremely significant effect on claims: driver age and gas type.
We will compare these models using 5-fold cross validation on the
metrics mean absolute error (MAE) and mean square error (MSE).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{PoliciesGLM[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}fold\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{] }\OtherTok{\textless{}{-}} \FunctionTok{cut}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{seq}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(PoliciesGLM)),}\AttributeTok{breaks=}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{,}\AttributeTok{labels=}\ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{crossValMetrics }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}

\begin{verbatim}
##                     avgMAE     avgMSE
## Poisson         0.08896751 0.04511406
## PoissonNoArea   0.08896388 0.04511421
## PoissonBaseline 0.08953675 0.04539566
\end{verbatim}

The baseline model outperforms the more complicated ones in MAE, but
falls short in MSE. Using squares means that MSE is more sensitive to
outliers, and while we have tried to control for outliers that make
little sense, a model's performance in extreme situations will be a big
part of its usefulness in the insurance industry. We will select the
second model to do our final evaluation on.

\section{Model evaluation}\label{model-evaluation}

We will evaluate our final model by training it on all of the training
data and computing MSE on two versions of the test data: one with the
filters on exposure and claim number applied, and one on the raw data.
We will compare these results to the ones from earlier cross-evaluation.
